items.question: How is JavaScript different from TypeScript and C# at run time?
items.answer: JavaScript is dynamically typed and executed by an engine such as V8 in the browser or Node.js. TypeScript only type-checks before compile; types erase to plain JavaScript the engine never sees. C# compiles to Intermediate Language (IL) with Common Type System (CTS) metadata, and the Common Language Runtime (CLR) enforces types at run time on threads — not on a single-threaded event loop. Same JSON payload in a Node Lambda versus a .NET Lambda means different hosts, garbage collectors, and type systems.
followUps: Does typeof in JavaScript mean the same as GetType() in C#?
What survives tsc that does not survive Roslyn?
items.sixtySeconds: JS: dynamic types on V8. TS erases. C#: IL plus CLR metadata on threads. Same JSON, different runtime. Never collapse the three layers.

items.question: Explain how V8 compiles JavaScript — is it interpreted or compiled?
items.answer: Modern V8 is Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled, not purely interpreted. Source parses to an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), Ignition generates bytecode that runs immediately, and hot functions promote to TurboFan optimized machine code. If run-time types or object shapes diverge from what the optimizer assumed, V8 deoptimizes back to bytecode. Unlike the CLR, V8 lacks IL metadata and must speculate from observed values. Benchmark after warm-up — cold bytecode is not steady-state performance.
followUps: What is a hidden class and why does property order matter?
When does deoptimization hurt production latency?
items.sixtySeconds: Parse, bytecode, profile, TurboFan, deopt. Not interpreted-only. Warm up benchmarks. CLR has metadata upfront; V8 infers.

items.question: What is the difference between the call stack and the scope chain?
items.answer: The call stack is a last-in-first-out structure of active function execution contexts — who is running right now. The scope chain is lexical: inner functions look up names in outer environments based on where they were written, not who called them. A closure captures the outer lexical environment on the heap, so variables survive after the outer function's stack frame pops. C# closures work similarly via compiler-generated classes, but without JavaScript hoisting or temporal dead zone quirks.
followUps: Why does for (var i) with setTimeout log 3 three times?
What is the temporal dead zone for let?
items.sixtySeconds: Stack = active calls LIFO. Scope chain = lexical nesting. Closures keep outer env on heap, not stack frames. var hoists; let has TDZ.

items.question: What does strict mode change, and when is it on by default?
items.answer: Strict mode turns silent mistakes into thrown errors: assignments to undeclared identifiers throw ReferenceError instead of creating globals, delete on non-configurable properties throws, duplicate parameter names are a syntax error, and this in unbound functions is undefined instead of the global object. ES modules and class bodies are strict automatically. Classic scripts without 'use strict' run in sloppy mode. C# enforces equivalent rules at compile time — there is no opt-in toggle.
followUps: Does 'use strict' inside a block enable strict for that block?
How does strict mode affect arguments aliasing parameters?
items.sixtySeconds: Strict: no implicit globals, undefined this in plain functions, modules always strict. Sloppy allows globals. C# catches at compile.

items.question: Predict the console output: sync logs, setTimeout(0), and Promise.then — in what order?
items.answer: Synchronous code runs first while the call stack is active. When the stack empties, the event loop drains all microtasks — promise .then handlers and await continuations — before taking the next macrotask such as setTimeout. Classic puzzle: console.log('1'); setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3')); console.log('4'); prints 1, 4, 3, 2. async/await splits functions at await boundaries into the same microtask scheduling.
followUps: Where does process.nextTick fit in Node compared to microtasks?
Does await create a new thread?
items.sixtySeconds: Sync first. All microtasks. One macrotask. Repeat. setTimeout is not instant. async is promise microtasks. JS single-threaded.

items.question: Why is JavaScript called single-threaded, and how does it still handle I/O?
items.answer: Each JavaScript realm has one call stack executing one function at a time on one thread. The host — browser or Node.js — uses non-blocking operating system APIs and places completion callbacks on task queues. The event loop runs those callbacks when the stack is clear. Long synchronous CPU work blocks everything including UI and timers. Parallel CPU requires Web Workers or worker_threads — separate isolates with message passing. C# uses thread pools and Task scheduling; async I/O frees threads rather than blocking one loop.
followUps: What happens if you busy-wait for three seconds on the main thread?
How do Workers differ from shared-memory threads?
items.sixtySeconds: One stack per realm. Host does async I/O. Loop schedules callbacks. CPU blocks loop. Workers for parallel CPU. C# uses thread pool.

items.question: How do ES modules differ from classic script tags in the browser?
items.answer: ES modules (type=module) are always strict, have their own top-level scope so var does not become a global, load with defer semantics by default, and resolve static import/export at parse time before evaluation. Classic scripts run in sloppy mode unless 'use strict' is present, top-level var attaches to globalThis, and blocking scripts halt HTML parsing unless defer or async. import in JavaScript loads and evaluates code — unlike C# using which only shortens names.
followUps: What is top-level await and when is it allowed?
Why do cross-origin module scripts need CORS?
items.sixtySeconds: Modules: strict, deferred, module scope, import graph. Scripts: global var, sloppy default. import runs code; C# using does not.

items.question: Your Node service mixes require and import — what breaks and how do you fix it?
items.answer: require and static import cannot coexist in the same file — it is a syntax error. CommonJS (.cjs or no type module) uses synchronous require and module.exports. ES modules (.mjs or package.json type module) use import/export with strict mode and live bindings. Fix by choosing one format per package boundary, using dynamic import() from CommonJS when needed, or configuring dual package exports carefully. TypeScript emit target must match runtime — tsc to ESM requires Node ESM mode.
followUps: What is the difference between default export interop in CJS versus ESM?
How do circular ESM imports behave at evaluation?
items.sixtySeconds: No require plus import same file. CJS synchronous. ESM strict with live bindings. Pick per package. Dynamic import() bridges from CJS.
